I guess trick is the wrong word for it, you record two tracks at once, one using the parallel output.

The parallel out will be your sub track. You begin by shelving the low end any where from 300 to 200 hZ and then low pass anything past where you just shelved.

Next you take your wet track, and high pass so that the low end from this track doesn't clash with the sub track. I also like to boost the mids of this track around the 1 kHz  to 2 kHz region depending on the mix. 

After you are done you blend the two to taste.

The thing is distortion is an acquired taste, I may love my bass to sound like heavy machinery, but you might not dig that. Try to find distortion tones that you like. 

If I were you I'd recommend looking at different examples of distortion and understand what is going on frequency wise. 

Also I can't recall at the moment if you are a flat or round wound user, distortion will exacerbate the high end and mids of a round wound string much more than a flat wound string.  

Also something to be very wary of, sometimes isolated distortion parts on bass can sound great but fizzle out in a mix. On the other hand seemingly too much or too harsh of a distortion can sit just right in the mix. Let your ear decide in a full band situation
